text: 44-year-old male. The patient's daughter reports a 1-week history of right leg weakness, unsteady gait, and multiple falls. Over the past 6 months, the patient has been increasingly forgetful, losing his way on familiar routes and facing difficulties operating simple kitchen appliances. He has also been paranoid, agitated, and restless recently.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma (PCNSL)

The patient's age (44), subacute progression over 6 months with prominent cognitive/behavioral changes (dementia, paranoia), and new focal neurological deficits (weakness, ataxia) combined with leukopenia strongly suggest an infiltrative malignancy rather than a demyelinating disease like MS, which typically presents with distinct relapsing-remitting episodes of optic neuritis or sensory deficits. The "nonenhancing" nature of the lesions on initial MRI can occur in PCNSL, particularly in immunocompromised states or early stages, but the clinical picture is highly atypical for multiple sclerosis given the rapid cognitive decline and focal weakness. I will proceed with a lumbar puncture to analyze cerebrospinal fluid for malignant cells and cytology to confirm the diagnosis.
